fact: Roofs and paving can be far hotter than the air, and these surface heat islands are strongest by day; US city air runs about 0.6–3.9 °C warmer by day and 1.1–2.8 °C at night on average (EPA). Neighbourhoods in one city differ by several degrees. Much of the night-time heat island is thermal inertia: heat trapped in urban surfaces by day is released at night. Tree shade can cool asphalt by 14–23 °C, yet a Boston study found only about 0.07 °C of afternoon air cooling per extra 10 % canopy.

Sunlight is reflected, shaded or absorbed; plants spend part of it evaporating water; heat moves between surface, air, sky and mass; air mixes deeply with the region by day and weakly at night. A third run, open countryside, is the yardstick for the heat island. Settings are illustrative and chosen so results fall inside published ranges.
simulation: A deterministic day with fixed sunrise and sunset, starting from the first hot day after cooler weather, optionally repeated for three days. Every temperature, flow and stored-heat figure is generated in the browser. No real city, forecast, sensor, API, account, upload, backend or stored data is involved.
limitations: Temperature only: no humidity, heat index, human comfort or health risk, and not medical advice. No waste heat from air conditioning, vehicles or industry. Each block stands alone, so real district-wide cooling from trees or roofs is smaller than shown; the tree option is an upper bound. Plants are assumed well watered. Surface is a block average. Coastal, desert and humid cities behave differently.

fact: Historical snapshot: the figures below use USDA’s March 10, 2026 release of 2024 data, not the November 17, 2026 revision and new 2025 release. In 2024 U.S. farms received 18.5¢ of each dollar spent on food at home, 7.1¢ of each dollar spent on food away from home and 11.8¢ across all domestically produced food; the rest pays for processing, transport, storage, wholesale and retail. The farm share varies widely by food: 69.1¢ for fresh eggs, 52.2¢ for beef, 50.8¢ for fresh milk, 4.8¢ for bakery products. Salaries and benefits are 47.2¢ of the average grocery dollar. Because the farm share is small, large commodity swings move retail food prices less than people expect, and retail prices tend to follow commodity prices up faster than down. In 2024 the lowest-income fifth of U.S. households spent 33.0% of before-tax income on food, the middle fifth 12.2% and the highest fifth 6.4%.
model: Khizooology splits one dollar of each food into seven slices: the farm gate (USDA’s farm share) and six links after the farm (processing and packaging, transport and storage, wholesale, retail, energy, finance, ads and legal), dividing the post-farm share in proportion to USDA’s value added by industry group for that food. A cost shock grows one slice; with nothing else changing and full pass-through the shelf price rises by slice times shock. Wages use USDA’s salary-and-benefits figure, are shown as an extra block and are never added to the slices. The household panel multiplies a price rise by the share of income spent on food.
simulation: A deterministic slider from 0% to 100%, with a demo run from 0% to 50%. Every figure is computed in the browser from 2024 USDA numbers bundled in the page. No live price, forecast, API, account, upload, backend or stored data is involved.
limitations: A ceiling, not a prediction: it assumes the whole extra cost reaches the shelf at once, unchanged purchases and no absorbed profit. USDA shares are national averages. The split of the post-farm share across six links is this model’s assumption. Energy counts only after the farm. Profit, fairness, market power and demand shifts are not modelled. U.S. only: 2024 data from the March 10, 2026 release. USDA revised earlier years on November 17, 2026; these historical inputs are not the latest estimates. The household panel treats total food spending, eating out included, like groceries, so it is an upper bound and not financial advice.

fact: In a study of about 126,000 stories shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017, false stories spread farther and faster than true ones and were about 70% more likely to be reshared; they were also more novel. A 2021 re-analysis found that true and false stories reaching the same number of people spread the same way; the main difference was how often people passed them on. In large online datasets over 99% of sharing chains end within one step. Repeated statements are rated as more true, with the biggest jump at the second exposure. Corrections reduce belief in misinformation but work less well after repetition or delay, and better when they come from the original source.
model: A made-up town of 120 people in four neighborhoods of 30, each with about 6 friends, 8 friendships across neighborhoods and 3 hubs followed by 21 to 34 people. Each hour everyone who decided to share sends the post to all their connections; each person shares at most once. The first time someone sees it they pass it on with a 15% chance (10% when people check before sharing); a second sighting makes that ×1.5, a third or later ×1.7. The truth is posted by the same first poster and follows the same rules at the rumor’s share chance divided by 1.7. It sticks with a 70% chance that falls by a quarter for each extra time the person saw the rumor. Truth is never an input.
simulation: Every result is computed in the browser by a deterministic model. The story shows one fixed run, chosen because its results sit close to the average of 100 runs with different luck. No real platform, person, event, account, upload or backend is involved.
limitations: A toy town, not a real platform: no feeds, ranking algorithms, ads, groups or private chats, and everyone behaves alike. It tracks who heard what and who passed it on, not how strongly anyone believes it. The share chance, the repeat boost and the chance a correction sticks show the direction found in research; their sizes are simplified. Not a tool for judging whether a real claim is true, and not about any political topic.
status: Fact/model/source/limitation present; source-dependent claims reviewed proportionally, not an expert scientific validation
